lists.text:
1. Launch a citywide curbside compost collection program so food scraps are diverted from landfills.
2. Partner with grocery stores to donate unsold but safe food to local food banks.
3. Create a city-run app that alerts residents to discounted near-expiration food at nearby stores.
4. Run public education campaigns explaining the difference between "best by," "sell by," and "use by" labels.
5. Install community refrigerators in high-traffic neighborhoods where anyone can leave or take food.
6. Offer tax incentives to restaurants that track and reduce their kitchen waste.
7. Require large food businesses to separate organic waste from general trash.
8. Fund school programs that teach children about meal planning and food preservation.
9. Switch school cafeterias to "offer versus serve" so students choose only what they will eat.
10. Schedule recess before lunch in schools to reduce uneaten cafeteria food.
11. Establish a gleaning network that harvests leftover crops from nearby farms after the main harvest.
12. Support "ugly produce" markets that sell cosmetically imperfect fruits and vegetables at lower prices.
13. Provide free kitchen caddies and compostable bags to every household.
14. Build an anaerobic digester that converts food waste into biogas for city vehicles or electricity.
15. Host free community workshops on canning, pickling, fermenting, and freezing.
16. Encourage restaurants to offer smaller portion sizes at reduced prices.
17. Normalize take-home containers by asking restaurants to offer them proactively.
18. Create a volunteer food rescue corps that picks up surplus from events and delivers it to shelters.
19. Publicize Good Samaritan liability protections so businesses feel safe donating food.
20. Implement pay-as-you-throw trash pricing to reward households that produce less waste.
21. Open a city-supported commercial kitchen that turns rescued produce into soups and meals for social services.
22. Require city-catered events and meetings to arrange donation of leftover food.
23. Partner with local breweries to send spent grain to bakers or livestock farmers.
24. Help hospitals adopt room-service-style meal ordering to reduce untouched patient trays.
25. Distribute fridge thermometers and storage guides to help residents keep food fresher longer.
26. Hold a citywide "Waste Less Week" challenge with prizes for households that cut their food waste.
27. Encourage grocery stores to sell loose produce so shoppers can buy exact quantities.
28. Discourage bulk "buy one, get one free" promotions on perishables in favor of simple discounts.
29. Fund food waste audits for small businesses to identify where losses occur.
30. Provide grants for restaurants to buy smart scales that measure discarded food.
31. Create a public dashboard tracking the city's food waste diversion progress.
32. Install compost bins in community gardens and city parks.
33. Partner with local farms to accept food scraps for animal feed where regulations allow.
34. Support zero-waste restaurant certification with a public window decal.
35. Teach "cook it up" leftover recipes through library cooking demonstrations and online videos.
36. Distribute free meal-planning templates and shopping list guides at libraries and community centers.
37. Encourage universities to remove trays from dining halls to reduce over-serving.
38. Establish drop-off compost sites for apartment dwellers without curbside service.
39. Connect farmers' market vendors with charities to take unsold produce at the end of market day.
40. Encourage grocers to use dynamic pricing that automatically discounts items as they near expiration.
41. Support local startups that turn food byproducts into new products like flour from juice pulp.
42. Offer city-backed cold storage for small food pantries that cannot store perishables.
43. Train food service workers in inventory rotation practices like "first in, first out."
44. Ban organic waste from landfills on a phased timeline with support for affected businesses.
45. Promote cafeteria share tables where students can leave unopened items for others.
46. Give finished compost back to residents free for their gardens to reinforce participation.
47. Coordinate with apartment managers to add compost chutes or bins in multi-family buildings.
48. Recruit neighborhood "food waste ambassadors" to answer questions and encourage participation.
49. Include food waste reduction goals in the city's official climate action plan.
50. Partner with delivery apps to promote surplus "mystery bags" of unsold food from local bakeries and cafés.

lists.text:
1. Launch a citywide curbside compost collection program that accepts all food scraps from residential households.
2. Require grocery stores above a certain size to donate edible unsold food to food banks or charities.
3. Offer tax incentives to restaurants that track and publicly report reductions in their food waste.
4. Fund a public awareness campaign explaining the difference between "best by," "sell by," and "use by" labels.
5. Partner with a food-rescue app that lets residents buy surplus restaurant and bakery meals at a discount.
6. Install community refrigerators in neighborhoods where residents can freely leave and take safe, unexpired food.
7. Switch school cafeterias to an "offer versus serve" model so students take only the items they intend to eat.
8. Schedule school lunch after recess so children arrive hungry and eat more of their meals.
9. Create share tables in school cafeterias where students can leave unopened items for classmates.
10. Provide free kitchen countertop compost bins to households that sign up for food scrap collection.
11. Host monthly "fix your fridge" workshops teaching residents how to store produce so it lasts longer.
12. Establish a municipal grant program for nonprofits that run refrigerated food rescue vehicles.
13. Implement pay-as-you-throw trash pricing so households pay less when they divert food from landfill.
14. Encourage farmers markets to sell "imperfect" produce at reduced prices near the end of each market day.
15. Organize volunteer gleaning teams to harvest unpicked crops from nearby farms and orchards for donation.
16. Build or contract an anaerobic digester that converts commercial food waste into biogas and fertilizer.
17. Ban food waste from commercial landfill disposal for large generators like hotels, hospitals, and supermarkets.
18. Offer free waste audits to restaurants to identify where and why food is being discarded.
19. Encourage restaurants to offer smaller portion sizes at lower prices as a standard menu option.
20. Normalize take-home containers by requiring restaurants to offer them proactively to diners.
21. Clarify and publicize Good Samaritan liability protections so businesses feel safe donating food.
22. Create a city-run online platform matching businesses with surplus food to nearby charities in real time.
23. Train hospital and nursing home kitchens in demand-forecasting to prepare meals closer to actual need.
24. Introduce room-service-style ordering in hospitals so patients choose meals when they are hungry.
25. Partner with local breweries and bakeries to send spent grains and stale bread to farms as animal feed.
26. Support community gardens that accept neighborhood food scraps for on-site composting.
27. Run a "Clean Plate Challenge" competition between city schools with prizes for the biggest waste reductions.
28. Integrate food waste lessons into the public school science and home economics curriculum.
29. Offer free meal-planning templates and shopping list apps promoted through the city website and libraries.
30. Require city-catered events and meetings to use accurate headcounts and donate leftovers afterward.
31. Encourage supermarkets to discount near-expiry items with clearly marked "eat me first" sections.
32. Persuade grocery stores to eliminate "buy one, get one free" deals on perishables in favor of simple price cuts.
33. Fund a commercial kitchen where volunteers turn rescued produce into soups, sauces, and frozen meals.
34. Support local businesses that make products like jams, juices, or chips from surplus or blemished produce.
35. Provide drop-off compost sites at transit stations and libraries for residents in apartment buildings.
36. Mandate food scrap collection services in new multifamily residential developments.
37. Train food bank staff and volunteers to sort and redistribute perishables faster to reduce spoilage.
38. Offer cold storage space in city facilities to food pantries that lack adequate refrigeration.
39. Coordinate with grocery distributors to redirect rejected shipments to food banks rather than dumpsters.
40. Publish an annual city food waste report with measurable goals and progress tracking.
41. Host neighborhood "community supper" events cooked entirely from rescued food.
42. Encourage universities to adopt trayless dining, which has been shown to reduce plate waste.
43. Provide grants for restaurants to buy vacuum sealers, blast chillers, and other preservation equipment.
44. Partner with local chefs to create a public video series on cooking with leftovers and food scraps.
45. Promote "root-to-stem" and "nose-to-tail" cooking through restaurant week themes and menus.
46. Set up a seasonal canning and preserving class series at community centers during harvest peaks.
47. Give households free fridge thermometers and stickers showing the optimal temperature for food storage.
48. Encourage workplaces to designate a shared fridge cleanout day with leftovers offered to colleagues first.
49. Require city procurement contracts for food services to include waste-reduction and donation clauses.
50. Create a Food Waste Reduction Coordinator position in city government to oversee and integrate all these efforts.
